utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, Mr. Vukasinovic, that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vukasinovic. Your Honours, before we resume, there's something about yesterday's transcript, it's about one of my questions. I think the English interpretation was all right. It was probably a typo, so the question is unintelligible, page 14991, line 13, my question was, Mr. Vukasinovic, which rank did you hold at the time? The question was: "Was your rank at the time Major?" And the answer was "Yes." And the English was reads "Your rank of the time was that of imagine." The page is 14991, and the line is 13. Sir, Mr. Vukasinovic, the interpreters asked me yesterday after the hearing to make longer breaks between questions and answers and to try to go at a steadier pace. Therefore, please try to exercise some control over your pace, so that we don't run into any trouble regarding the interpretation. You told us yesterday about your tasks as town commander in terms of such information as who was coming and who was going in your area of responsibility, the village of Negoslavci. You say you were aware of the fact that people from the international community visited. My next question is about that. Do you know if any journalists came to Negoslavci or to the area of combat operations? If so, what exactly was the regime of their visits, if any, to the area covered by your town command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came during the fighting, especially as the operations were nearing a conclusion. Their visits were authorised through our superior command, needless to say. I would get all the names of any teams due to arrive and then I would simply let them in. At the time, there was a press centre in a building in Negoslavci. That's where they would go and where the relevant officers received them and took them anywhere they'd ask to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which particular officer was in charge of that press centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of establishment, it was the assistant commander for moral guidance, Lieutenant Marko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Radojica Sforca mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot to mention him. He was one of the officers who was in charge of communicating with journalists, to be at the centre, to receive journalists and to take them wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The rank was Colonel Marko Maric, not lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the relationship between your own security organ of the Guards Brigade - the OTP referred to that as operation group - at any rate, between your department and the other security bodies present within the territory of OG South or within OG South itself as a unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That relationship was of a collegial nature. We weren't their superiors, and they weren't our superiors. We each had our own respective areas of responsibility, and we were all in charge of our own units. They sent their reports to their own superior officer. What was -- when it was really important for any of their tasks within the area of combat operations, they could have gone to the chief of security of Operations Group South for assistance, if needed in terms of assessing certain situations, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any activities that you had yourself with any other security bodies within the area covered by OG South? Did you have any contact like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once the 20th Partisan Brigade arrived in the operations zone, and I was told to go to call all the security officers and to inform them about the situation that prevailed along the front line, especially as concerned their own security measures and counter-intelligence difficulties that we were encountering. Any unit, when arriving in a zone of combat operations, must be met by someone who will then introduce them into combat and explain to them what the situation was, and that is precisely what I did in the case of the arrival of the 20th Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember in which sector they were stationed when you contacted them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the Ovcara/Jakubovac sector, in that general area. Their command was in the Ovcara sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if they, the security officers of the 20th Partisan Brigade, at any point in time submitted any reports to you regarding their own activities, submitted them to you as a security officer of OG South or the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me personally. But if you consider what I said a moment ago, I am certain that they submitted such reports to their own superior, and their superior would have been part of the 1st Military District. Did the commander of that particular unit need to seek assistance from the commander of OG South or through his own chief of security, Mr. Sljivancanin? I don't know. If any assistance was sought or received, then Mr. Sljivancanin must know, I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at Exhibit 841. Can we please have that brought up on our screens. Mr. Vukasinovic, my question: Do you remember, after the Vukovar operation, being involved in compiling a list? We've been looking at that document over the last few days; just a glance, and we can see what that is about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have that slightly enlarged please? That's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Can we please first have page two and then we'll go back to page 1, the lower half of page 2. Mr. Vukasinovic, tell us what you know about this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I wrote. Normally, after the conclusion of any combat activities, one analyses assignments, one assesses any weaknesses that occurred, in terms of using one's own units and conducting combat operations. Another assessment is made is that of equipment and weapons. In one word, anything that affected the course of combat. As I was in charge, in charge of looking after those military police units, in charge of making assessments regarding their combat readiness, my assignment, the assignment that I received, was to write down any observations that I made regarding the use of military police units in the fighting in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on what do you claim in this document that you took part in the -- in producing this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have my initials right there, Ljubisa Vukasinovic, LJV, That is the person who actually wrote the document. ZM, the following initials, is the person who typed that report; and on the right-hand side, you have the signature of the officer who eventually signed the report, in this case, Lieutenant-Colonel Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to page 1, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript, page 5, line 21, B/C/S, the witness said LJV.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: LJ is a single letter and sound in B/C/S, which does not exist in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please pull the document up a little. We need the portion that is midway down the page. A little further up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a single question in relation to this document which seems to be self-explanatory. Halfway down the page, we see this: "The quarter master's uniforms are not appropriate for carrying out assignments in a settled area, in a populated area, especially the M-77-type uniform." My question: How did members of -- what did members of the military police of the Guards Brigade wear? What sort of uniforms during the actual fighting, and were these uniforms in any way different than those worn by other brigades that were part of OG South?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military composition of military police units, or rather, the men of military police units were wearing M-77 uniforms. The anti-terrorist company and some of its officers were wearing what was commonly referred to at the time as camouflage uniforms. All the other units within the zone of combat operations wore either M-77 or another older type of uniform, so the-called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness or the expression that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last word, what exactly did you use? The old type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a uniform made of wool.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the other members of military police units wear the same types of uniform as those in the Guards Brigade during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had M-77, white belts; and when fighting, they would wear grey ones. But the military police insignia are clearly displayed on the grey one, too. So the change in colour didn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to what we really want to know at this trial, the 18th, the 19th and the 20th of November. Mr. Vukasinovic, we take the 18th of November as the date when combat operations ceased, for the purposes of this trial. Do you still remember what you did on the 18th of November? I was trying not to lead you. I don't want to know about the whole day. What I want to know is that do you know that the Mitnica group surrendered on that day, and is there anything that you did about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain in the briefest possible terms what happened. After combat operations were successfully brought to an end along that axis, there were negotiations and a surrender of the Croatian forces along that axis was agreed. Colonel Pavkovic was party to those negotiations. The negotiations were successful that day, and a surrender of the Mitnica battalion at Mitnica was agreed. I arrived there sometime in the afternoon. I had been informed that there was a flood of people that started coming in after the surrender of the Mitnica battalion, and the civilians living in that neighbourhood started showing up in great numbers. Word had got through to the command already. So the security commander summoned me to go there and help with the security situation, in terms of helping to pull people out and in terms of putting up such large numbers of people. Between two and a half thousand and 3.000 people in my estimate, perhaps more. It's very difficult to be very specific about what happened at the time, because it has been a long time. It's very difficult to pinpoint the exact point in time at which certain things happened back then. It is a problematic exercise. However, I do remember the event itself, and I can, in general terms, say what it was about. I arrived there to see my chief, Mr. Sljivancanin. I saw a large number of people there, a huge crowd, and something had to be done in order to put them up and meet their needs. The commander was informed, and he immediately took action to send vehicles over. Four fighters had surrendered, and civilians alike. So now there were a lot of lorries there and buses in order to have people evacuated from the Vucedol and Mitnica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the area in which you were at that moment with Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Vucedol. It is to the south from the place where the Mitnica group surrendered, so the name is Vucedol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay at Vucedol, did anything else happen that you can recall? Did anyone come to see you there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember quite well. It was already dusk. Night was falling when a courier brought a telegram, or rather, an envelope with a cable in it which he handed over to Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was in the telegram? Did you have occasion to see the content of that telegram? And please do slow down, Mr. Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did have occasion to see it. It was a coded telegram; and also in the meanwhile, Sljivancanin himself told me what the content of it was. In principle, I can retell you what it was. They said that -- it said that a large number of our men and officers were prisoners of the Croatian forces; and that it was necessary, if possible, to ensure a number of persons for the purpose of exchange. So that was the gist of it, the content of the telegram, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was anyone -- anyone's signature below the telegram?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature was that of Aca Vasiljevic, the then chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, during that day, did you, and if so when, go to Ovcara? At what time of day, if you can remember? You don't have to give us the exact time, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before I do that, there is something else I have to say. Sljivancanin said - and I remember his words well - he said to me, he said: "Vukasin," and that is how everybody called me, "Look at the number of people here. We need to look after all these people," and that was the basic task. How to go about pulling out these frightened people who practically, without any clothes, to take them out of the area, pull them out, and see to their needs. That took some time. You know how it was, that people were upset. They were anxious; they were frightened. Everybody wanted to go somewhere, so that that took us sometime in order to establish some sort of order and calm and to start loading the people on to the buses, talk to them, and so on. So that took a while. In addition to that, we had problems with people who had gone out with their own private cars and who insisted that they sit off in their respective directions in their cars. But that was not possible to secure, to ensure, in view of the fact that combat operations were still in progress. We told them that we would be organising, in the Ovcara area, this space where they could rest and wait for further decisions in terms of where they would be transported. They were all transported as far as Ovcara; and when we arrived at Ovcara, the area of the command. The so-called yellow house and the -- this road towards the hangars, there were buses parked there; and on a meadow right by the road, to the right-hand side, was a spot where they ordered that they park all their private cars and leave the keys in the cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you approximately tell us what the number of cars was involved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I believe that there were about 30 or 40 cars there; different vehicles, different makes, mostly of domestic make: Zastavas, perhaps a Mercedes or two. It was quite late. Actually, I think it was about 2200 or 2300 hours. I know that it was very late when we had regulated the entire situation and prepared for the command to take measures and send other organs that would be leading the convoy in other directions towards Serbia and so on. It was very late.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with this last answer of yours, do you know whether these civilians were offered to go to Croatia, if any of them wanted to go to Croatia, and others offered to go to Serbia if that is what they wanted? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We asked them. They were asked and they were all put on the convoy for which they opted, and we actually accommodated their wishes. That was the least that we could do for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The civilians who have come in their private cars, that left their cars there, did they leave Ovcara that evening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A number were transported to Sremska Mitrovica and Sid; and a number of them went towards Velepromet. That is how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how long did you stay, if you can, at Ovcara that evening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, assessing the time it took for us to complete all those activities, I believe that we stayed there for about six or seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Sljivancanin with you that evening at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were there until the entire situation was resolved and the people put on the buses and the convoys had set off; then I went to the village of Negoslavci with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we should move on to the 19th of November. Do you remember, is there anything that makes you remember your activities on the 19th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 19th of November was a day that was quite rife with activities, starting with the visit of Mr. Cyrus Vance, a representative of the United Nations in the morning. This was a very important visit so that we needed to take certain measures in order for the visit to take place, which it, of course, had its purpose. And our task was to create the necessary security conditions for Mr. Cyrus Vance and the rest of his delegation to be protected against any possible influences. I received Mr. Cyrus Vance; not I personally, but my forces already at Sid. He was transported in our combat vehicle to the village of Negoslavci, to the command of the OG South, where he spent a certain time with the commander and the rest of the command members. And then, having been given a security escort, he was then further transported to the barracks in Vukovar, and I don't know what his further activities were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you know only about what happened in the area of Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is in connection with that visit, and I'm not going to ask you any further questions about that. My next question is: During that day, did you see Mr. Sljivancanin and, if so, when; and what was the theme of your encounter, of your meeting? What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would meet, as I said, usually after the briefing. During that talk -- first of all, he wanted to know and asked me how Mr. Cyrus Vance had been received, and what he had said in connection with the situation that he had observed and the measures that we had taken. He told me that he was satisfied with how we had received him and the preparations that we had undertaken and the guarantees and security that we had provided for him under very difficult circumstances. Most importantly, at that moment, I informed him of some other problems, which had cropped up on the 19th of November, that he had not been aware of. All our convoys that had been sent towards Croatia returned in the afternoon about 6.00 or 7.00 p.m. in the afternoon, because the Croatian forces would not let them in. And this one convoy that had been returned from Zupanja was stationed at Ovcara again. So there were problems associated with that; namely, to secure food and water for those people to be able to make it through the night until the next morning. And the commander undertook every possible step to ensure that water and food was taken to them; but I told him that despite all that, the Croatian forces and the Croatian authorities were creating problems for us, because they were returning their own population. So I wanted to inform him of that so that he might know what the problems were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a little bit, we will follow-up on that topic a bit later. What I would like to know at this point is whether you talked about the evacuation of the hospital at all at that point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We talked about the evacuation of the hospital, but that was later when I informed him of the problems and when I informed him of the problems with the cars that had remained there. As for the second part, after having listened to me, he told me that we had a difficult, serious task ahead of us, in which I was tasked with doing certain things. On the following day, on the 20th, he had tasked me with preparing the buses, reporting at the hospital where I was to take persons who had been selected, and transport them to the Vukovar barracks. After all of them were transported, I was to organise a convoy for Sremska Mitrovica. That was a very detailed and specific task that I received from him that evening. So by your leave, let me repeat it. I was told to go to the hospital with a certain number of buses to take people who had been selected at the hospital, to transport them to the Vukovar barracks, to organise security there, and organise the convoy, and then dispatch that convoy towards Sremska Mitrovica. That was my main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to the task that you had for the following day, did Mr. Sljivancanin mention the word "Ovcara" at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no mention of Ovcara. The task was extremely clear, to transport people from the hospital to the Vukovar barracks. Ovcara was something we didn't even dream of, as we say in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was supposed to secure, or rather, provide buses on the 20th, now that we're dealing with this task?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that was most likely regulated at the command. At any rate, the buses were supplied by the chief of traffic service, Lieutenant-Colonel Loncar. He supplied me with buses. The military policemen came from the 2nd Military Police Battalion, that was the other component. So all of that was ready for me, prepared for me in front of my command post in Negoslavci. I simply got into my vehicle and then I proceeded with implementation of my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That evening conversation you had with Sljivancanin on the 19th, did you discuss the number of buses? Did you mention the number of buses, the number of persons, or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know anything about the numbers. The numbers were not discussed at all. We simply said that we needed to prepare vehicles in order to transport the selected persons. Nobody had any clue as to how many such persons there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about this term, "selected persons." In the previous period of time, you, as a security organ, did you have any knowledge about the persons located in the hospital, and what purposes the hospital was used for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had knowledge about that, that's natural. Our superior administration, security administration continuously sent to the chief of security information that they had received concerning the situation and certain counter-intelligence measures that had been undertaken and generally about this situation in our area of combat operations. Thus, such information continuously arrived, continuously arrived to us. And after the fall of Vukovar, a large number of the ZNG members, who did not wish to surrender and were given an opportunity to do so, in a way, camouflaged themselves. They hid in the hospital and in several other facilities in addition to the hospital. So we knew that at the hospital, there were members of the ZNG who had discarded their weapons, changed their clothes, and used the hospital as a means of getting out of the town via the International Red Cross. We also had information that we collected ourselves. We wiretapped certain conversations. We had our own sources of obtaining information. So, yes, we knew that there were people who had refused to surrender and who had chosen this means of fleeing. They disguised themselves as hospital personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was this: When you said earlier "selected persons," persons who were singled out, were those the persons whom you were supposed to transport from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of those who were not wounded, were not patients, or were not hospital staff were the persons whose identity had to be established, because there were too many people in the hospital who didn't actually belong there. Therefore, there was a danger that if we didn't do it, there would be an incident. There would be trouble, and those were the security measures that needed to be done when the wounded were evacuated. Had we failed to do that, there was the potential for a problem to arise and that was part of the task for the security organ; namely, to ensure that everything that needed to be done with the wounded and with the patients was done in the safest possible way, so that it would also be safe for our forces taking part in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you talked to Sljivancanin, did you have any information as to whether the units of OG South had already been at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our units had arrived there sometime at noon, 11.00 or 12.00. I knew, and I saw later when I came there. I saw them implementing their task; that was our unit from the 2nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Ovcara that evening and, if so, when and with whom?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was at Ovcara that evening, on the 19th in the evening. Due to what I have earlier told you about, telling Sljivancanin about that convoy and the persons, the convoy that had returned. And I told him that we had certain problems with private cars that were in it. And this is why we went there to see what measures had been taken up there and to see how that problem could be resolved, how those vehicles, cars could be removed from that position, because we had insufficient forces, security forces. And there was a risk, at that time, that it would be taken over by people who were unable to do that. That is to say, it was risky to leave vehicles up there because there was a risk of them being stolen or looted. After the briefing, after all the these discussions, he and I went there together to observe the situation, to survey the situation. It lasted about 20 minutes, half an hour. We got there. This was the sector of another unit, and their patrol stopped us. When they were given authorisation to let us in, we entered the area and an officer awaited us there who reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there next to the vehicles, and I was analysing the situation, how to resolve that problem with these vehicles that had remained there. They walked on the path towards buses, towards hangars, and they talked about something. I don't know about what. At any rate, after about some 20 minutes of conversation with him, the major came back and said that everything was fine there and that we had to resolve the issue with the vehicles by organising for them to be transported to Velepromet on the following day, because it was very risky. And he concluded that it was better for them to remain there that night. So that's how the situation was resolved. We got into our car and drove back to Negoslavci. I went to my command post, and he went to his.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you saw any of the TO members there on that occasion, any TO members of the Vukovar TO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. There were several people there, but I wouldn't be able to identify them. There were perhaps seven to eight of them, because they were, in general, interested in picking out vehicles. And Sljivancanin talked to them about that. He told them that nobody was allowed to take those vehicles, that those vehicles were temporarily requisitioned, and that no private persons were allowed to take them. That these vehicles would go to Velepromet, because Velepromet had been designated as a centre for such property.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you something of general nature before these events of 18th and 19th. Did you know Miroljub Vujevic and Stanko Vujanovic at the time? Did you have any contact with them? I'm talking now about the events before the 18th. Just a minute, please. We have an error interpretation into English, page 18, line 14. My question was: Did you know Miroljub Vujevic and Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to know somebody is a very vague term. I saw them a couple of times initially before the combat operations actually commenced. Once they got involved in combat, I didn't see them. But I saw them prior to that, five or six times in passing. Otherwise, we did not know each other. Personally, we did not have any detailed conversations. However, I had heard and I knew that they existed as such, and that they led certain units or combat groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Milan Lancuzanin, nicknamed Kameni? He was in charge of the Leva Supoderica detachment, does this mean much to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said pertains to all three of them. I heard of them. I maybe even saw them a couple of times. I knew that these two were commanders of the Petrova Gora detachment, and that Kameni was the commander of the Leva Supoderica detachment. That's what people used to call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now going to turn to the events on the 20th. You were quite active on that day, so let us start with the morning. What do you remember? Is there anything memorable about the 20th of November in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the passage of time, I'll try to be as brief in my description and to tell you what I remember and what, according to my recollections, is realistic and truthful. It is difficult to remember all that now. I continuously prepared myself, thought about this, contemplated this. But to tell you the truth, it's been so many years that it's somewhat difficult to give a proper answer. And I know that I'm required to give such an answer, so that the Trial Chamber can properly rule on this. So I will do my best to tell you how this transpired, and what my role and position in all of that was. On the 19th in the evening, having completed my conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin, I received the task that I told you about. On the 20th in the morning, sometime at around 6.00; that is to say, quite early. Because later on, it was more difficult once the units got active and started moving about. I got up quite early, because I wanted to get to the hospital early. So I took six military buses, whose drivers were civilians, and there were two military policemen on each bus. I headed the column in a Puch vehicle with a driver, and we went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please. I want to be sure that we get everything. Please slow down. Where did you take over the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses awaited me -- awaited me in front of my command post in Negoslavci on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were the military policemen at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in front of your command post, we had six buses; and on each bus, there were already two policemen; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I arrived at the hospital. En route, the road leading to the hospital was damaged by shells. There were all kinds of obstacles on that road; however, we passed through, and we crossed the bridge, which had been partially damaged, and we came to the hospital. I parked the buses there on that road in front of the gate. I parked the buses in rows in a line right next to the fence. They were parked in a military line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to put a photograph on the screen so the witness can describe it. This is from Exhibit 170, photograph number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please hand the witness a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you could please draw for us, based on your recollection, where they were parked. This is the Vukovar Hospital, right? You can draw on the screen itself.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this huge building, in the middle, is the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, sir. It means nothing to us when you point like that. We don't get to see that. You will have to actually draw on the image, and it will turn up on our screens. Can you please show, or rather, mark where the buses were parked, based on your recollection.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here, next to the fence. Between this small house and this point over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll talk later about the people getting on the buses, but could you please mark that line with a number one.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the location in this image where the people were standing, who were later made to get on the buses, when you arrived. Can you please mark that on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the number two line. So it was right here. There's a steep stretch towards the hospital entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is not the ideal image for this purpose. You said it steeps towards the entrance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's some sort of a driveway for ambulances to approach the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have this photograph admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 859, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, the morning that you left Negoslavci, you were on the way to the hospital. Later on, after you had left the hospital, did you ever see any ICRC vehicles throughout that time, throughout this journey?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that morning. I didn't see any. When I arrived at the hospital, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic. The picture was not saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, there's a tiny bit of difficulty with our equipment. Could you please mark the position of the buses, and mark that with the number one again.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now, please, mark the position of those people that were due to get on the buses.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right here. Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness's memory seems to have improved during this second go. I seek that this photograph now be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The improved photograph will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did that get a number? I didn't realise. Of course. We can now proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, when you got as far as the hospital, what exactly was the situation that you found there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the hospital, I found the following situation: As for the area that I marked with the number two, there was a group of persons standing there that had been separated off. How many exactly, I don't know, but there was a group standing there. Across the way, in front of the buses and across the street, there was a group of TO members. At this point in time, there was nothing much going on, and this is the situation that I found when I came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time, where were you for most of this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the gate, most of the time. I was standing right next to that first bus between the first bus, the gate, and the pylon that was there, the street lighting. I was waiting for the moment when that first group would start heading towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any search being conducted there, those persons being searched; and, if so, who by? Any soldiers or officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No search was being conducted. The way I understand things to have happened, they were probably searched. But people were just standing there at this point, and no one was being searched. There's a concrete elevation by the road, and these people were lined up forming a sort of corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the hospital building itself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never entered the hospital building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time, did you ever enter the hospital yard?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I passed the swing gate, and I reached those first groups of persons who had been separated off, which is probably five or six metres into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there, did you see Sljivancanin; and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, I did not see him. I did see him later though. I saw him leave the hospital and go back several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "later," is that before the buses left or after? Did you see Sljivancanin at any point in time between your arriving and the time the first group was taken away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was after that first group was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the loading of persons on to buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a signal from Captain Simic that that group was now done and that they could start boarding. I took charge of that, and I personally got them to board the bus one-by-one, filling the seats as they went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Captain Simic. What do you think he was doing there, and what exactly was your contact about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he and his company were securing the hospital. It was that that I talked to him about. There was this group that had been screened, and he was saying something to the effect that I should now take charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any other officers there at roughly the same time, any other Guards Brigade or OG South officers, to be more specific?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I only remember my own colleagues, people who worked with me. There was Major Mladen Karan. I saw Radoje Paunovic. I saw Simic. I saw some of his commanders. I saw some people from our medical corps, some doctors and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that any officers had arrived on the previous day from the security administration, or did you personally meet them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't meet any. But if this occurred at the command post, it must have been recorded. A group of officers from the security administration arrived at the command post, and this was registered at our reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vukasinovic, what, precisely, were you wearing at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wearing a camouflage uniform. I had a pistol and a belt. I was wearing a NATO helmet. When I wasn't wearing one, I would normally wear a Tito cap with the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your superior, Veselin Sljivancanin? Was he wearing the same sort of camouflage uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same sort of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask my learned friend to be careful about the way he asks questions. That is about the third time. I would submit the structure of the question tends to suggest the answer and, therefore, is leading. The question that should have been asking was: "Do you know what uniform Mr. Sljivancanin was wearing?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are asked to be careful, Mr. Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, tell me this: How tall are you exactly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 190 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else about the loading of persons on to buses. As far as I understand, you say that you tried to fill the buses as they came; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this loading procedure, was there anyone else around, with the exception of the soldiers, the military policemen, and you, the officers? I'm talking about that area just outside the buses themselves.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one between the gate itself, the swing gate, and the buses, aside from my policemen and myself. Across the street at a distance of about ten or 15 metres, there was some TO men standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any TO men in the hospital courtyard during your time there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were none there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there, aside from buses, did you see any other vehicles parked there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were none, at least not along the stretch of the road where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Specifically, any ambulances?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were ambulances, but that was across the way on the opposite side of the hospital, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were there, did you see anyone being stretchered, as far as the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there with those buses, did you see any women outside the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Did you hear any threats being uttered against the people getting on to the buses, in the area in which you were standing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were exchanges; there were people muttering. But it was still quite early, so there was nothing special. There were cat calls and whistles, but not much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone utter the following words: "They will be swallowed by the dark in broad daylight." Does that phrase ring a bell, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there next to the buses, did you see Sljivancanin emerge in front of the buses and outside the hospital fence, the hospital perimeter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Bogdan Kuzmic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Darko Kovacevic, aka Drka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the fact that our next session will be a shorter one, and I'm about to move on to a different topic, maybe it would be convent for us to take an early break, because the next session will be concluded at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, the next session will be -- I beg your pardon, yes, 12.45, an hour earlier than on other days. We will then have the break now, Mr. Lukic. Quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My apologies that I was delayed on another matter, and we're back in court nearly 10 minutes late. All my fault. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, at a certain point in time, did you leave this area outside the hospital, and how did that happen? How did that go, in a couple words, and then we shall move on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I had all the three buses loaded, after I had filled all the three buses, as there was nobody else left there, I assessed that we should then move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. How many buses did you bring outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said that you enter as the buses came and filled the buses as they came?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to be leading, to suggest any answer to you. Tell me, how did you reach that decision? When did you reach that decision? How many buses left on the first group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this separated off group, the searched group, the already processed group, so to speak, when that was loaded, that bus left; and then I decided to load the other people and not to wait for the others. How many there would be, I wasn't sure. I decided to take them to Vukovar barracks, and this is what I did. I turned my vehicle and with those three buses, we set off towards Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many buses remained there in situ?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three buses remained there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want us to be precise. You know that I told you during the proofing that there were people who were claiming that all the six buses left at once. I have told you this before, and I want to ask you once again: Are you sure what you have just told us; namely, that you led in the first group three buses, that you led three loaded buses outside this first group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I'm quite positive about that, because I did it myself. And I'm the best placed person to do that, and I set here before you, Your Honours, that these other stories do not correspond to the truth, and that what I'm telling you is the precise account of the situation. I know what I did; namely, I drove, I took away three loaded buses with around 100, 150 people on them, and we took them in the direction of the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately at what time - we appreciate that you can't have the exact time, as you have already expressed your reservations in that connection - but what was the time, approximately, that you left towards the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that in some statements, but I suppose it was about 10.00 in the morning. It could be that time, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What direction did you take? What route did you take when moving towards the barracks, vis-a-vis the one when you were coming? Did you return to the barracks taking the same route, in other words?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One didn't have much choice. There was just this one route, and we took that same road across the bridge up to the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Mr. Vukasinovic, what time did you arrive at the barracks? Where did the buses stop, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got to the barracks, we passed through the checkpoint which was at the gate to the barracks. There was a ramp. There was a swing gate, which actually the ramp was outward and it was in vertical position. I entered the compound, the barracks compound; and had the bus drivers park the buses in a circular, round position, one behind another in a ring at a prescribed distance, one from another, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In what vehicle were you when this column left the hospital to go to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my Puch vehicle, and I led the column -- the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened after you arrived at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I arrived at the barracks and after the -- I had the buses parked, I immediately observed that the passenger vehicles were arriving with TO Vukovar members in them. So they left their vehicles outside and entered barracks compound on foot, and they just stood there outside the buses, opposite the buses. When I left my car, I saw that there were quite a few of them there. I could say an estimate between 30 and 40 TO members. So they stood there outside the buses on the side, and they started protesting and threatening, uttering threats at people in the buses whom they knew; probably their neighbours, former neighbours and friends whilst they had still been living in peace and at peace with each other. So they actually demonstrated that they recognised them and that they wanted to threaten them, in a way, for everything they had done at a certain point in the past to their neighbours. So they actually recognised some neighbours of theirs that they felt they had some scores to settle with, so that there was a crying out, cat calls and utterances of curses. And there was a big din.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they trying to get on the buses, to board the buses? Did they try to do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was perfectly aware that they wouldn't dare do that. The buses were closed; there were policemen at the bus doors. There was no possibility for them to break into the buses at all. That was totally ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just forgot to ask you a previous question. Let us hear what you have to say on that; namely, were those buses escorted, apart from military police also by officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the only officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As things evolved, what did you do? Did you take any steps, did you take any measures regarding the situation outside the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assessing the situation, I could see that they were being aggressive; and as the MP Company commander was there, Captain Predojevic, namely, who was in charge of security of the barracks, for securing the barracks, I called him. He was surprised at my arrival and the entry of these TO members into the compound. I told him that this was a task that had to be carried out during that day, and that we will be most probably organising a transport convoy to Sremska Mitrovica from that place. I told him that since I needed to go back to the hospital, that he needed to secure protection for the people in the buses, to prevent their being harassed in any way whatsoever, being approached, accessed in any way. So the people in the buses had to be secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear whether there were any other officers there at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear. We had the forward command post there, and the commander had set up his forward command post for the barracks before and after the fall of Vukovar. So Lukic was there and Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was also there, and they were probably in the barracks. I did not see them in the compound, but I presume that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MR. LUKIC: [Interpretation] The translation here says, "I presume," you said that "you knew" that they were there. I'm referring to Panic and Lukic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the forward command post. He was the commander of the forward command post, so it was presupposed that he would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But did you hear that Panic was there when you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that Panic was at the barracks, and I heard that from Mladen Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insisted right away, I insisted to see who the leader was among them, and I saw that that was the gentleman, Commander Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among whom when you say "among them," among which group were you trying to pinpoint that group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the TO group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him to bring pressure to bear on his combatants, to try to calm down the situation and actually get them out of the barracks. And I told him also that I had other obligations to discharge vis-a-vis the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was his reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was not much of a reaction on his part. He just stared blankly at me, like no big deal style. He didn't really react. And then I insisted that he really bring pressure to bear on his men, so they stop all this shouting and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a more serious clash between you and then at a certain point then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A more serious clash occurred at a moment when a driver -- actually, the driver of Mr. Sljivancanin arrived, and he brought a piece of paper, printed paper to me on which was written how many people should return to the hospital. It was a list, actually. And the list contained 20 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to the driver, "that is okay." I told him to bring up an empty bus, so that I would put these people, transfer them to that bus. In the meanwhile, I went from to bus to bus, called peoples' names out, to find those people and to see whether they were on any of those buses. Having found them all, I told them to approach the front door, and that I would be calling out one-by-one somewhat later to transfer them to the other bus, which had arrived in the meantime. They didn't know where they would be taken. They just heard that they should report, and they did report -- rather, respond as I called their names out. Once the bus arrived, I had it come closer, some ten metres closer, some halfway between the buses -- these buses in the middle of these buses, so that I could put these people in as quickly as possible. So I had people come out from the first bus, from the second bus, and from the third bus and put them on that bus. During that process of transferring people, there was even more arrogance manifested by the assembled persons, and some even tried to deliver a blow or two with their hands. They didn't wield any things, blunt instruments or something, but some individuals did receive a blow or two. I probably sustained a couple myself, and I really don't know how many. So that was a clash, and this is where we have this conflict. But I managed to overcome that problem, and eventually they desisted, perhaps waited for a different opportunity. I, however, waited for them to leave the barracks to go outside the compound. In the meantime, Mr. Vujovic actually left the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A number of questions about this and then we'll move on. Is there anything else you wanted to say, sir, about this fact that you moved the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just saying I took the bus back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're about to tackle that subject anyway, sir. As for that group of TO men who were voicing their displeasure, to put it that way, did you see any regular JNA soldiers standing among them, among that group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, the regular JNA troops were standing around the buses, sheltering them from being attacked by those people. As far as I was able to notice, I did not see any of our regular soldiers among them taunting or jeering. As far as I remember, no such thing occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of your fellow officers standing there, who were also jeering and who were acting in a rather passive way in this entire situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, there was no one, aside from myself and Mladen Predojevic. I don't know who any jeering officers might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I take it, based on your testimony, that as you were loading those people on to the buses, you were actually on the receiving end of a blow or two in that entire situation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm pretty strong, myself, so I took it in my stride.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your time in the barracks and before you again left for the hospital, did you see any lorries there, together with those buses or right next to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside the barracks, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None inside the barracks, no lorries. Quite the contrary, in fact. My own unit was there, the one from the barracks, the APCs, but that was a military police unit with their own equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For as long as you were in the barracks, did you ever realise that a van had driven up to where the buses were? Did you see anyone being taken off one of the buses, in circumvention of your previous decision and the people that you had, in fact, taken off?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. Not for as long as I was there, and there was no vehicles there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in the barracks, did you ever at any point see Mr. Sljivancanin there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the name of Milan Bulic, aka Bulija? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This empty bus that had arrived from the hospital, were there two military police officers on that bus as well? Do you remember sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to those policemen, did anyone else get on that bus, aside from the persons that you took there and put on the buses? Did any other soldiers or possibly TO men actually get on to that bus, with the exception of those military police officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happens next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just loaded 20 persons on to this bus, based on the list that I had. I now drove back to the hospital, and I left these persons just outside the gate. I saw a lot of medical staff there and other people too; and yet again, I spotted Vujovic, the TO commander, as well as Mr. Stanko Vujanovic, their former commander. I also came across the then Major Sljivancanin just outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This bus that you drove up in, what about those two other buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other two buses had been filled with the remaining persons who had been separated off. They were waiting on the buses, the doors were closed, and the policemen were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the people you returned to that area outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived with those people, Major Sljivancanin talked to each one of them about their release. He talked to each one individually, asked them about what they had done and where they had been. Each of them provided some guarantees. Everybody had somebody; the medical staff, the nurses, the doctors. Every time a person was brought up, they would give their opinion on that person, indicating whether they believed that person had been involved in some sort of criminal offence or in the actual fighting and whether that person should be released. He considered each of the cases in its own right. He sought everyone's approval; and whenever the conclusion was reached that someone was clean and not -- had not wronged anybody else, that person was released. Sometimes even the TO commanders would say: "He's all right. He's free to go." Three or four of them even spoke up to say that they had been involved in the fighting. They actually sent it themselves, so we just sent them back. I think Major Sljivancanin must have released at least 15 or 16 persons there who were ascertained to be innocent and in relation to whom who there was no further need to keep them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I want to go back to something in particular. When you came from the barracks to the hospital, did you tell Sljivancanin about what had gone on there? Did you inform him about that? Did you tell him about the facts that you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a little angry for the very first time. I was quite tolerant in certain situations, but this was very difficult for me to do. Under the circumstances, it was very difficult to get those people off the buses. I realise those are the people who were being arrogant, and I feared consequences. So I asked him that we should not do that sort of thing again. "There was no need," I said. It was hindering any further activity on our part and was inciting those TO men who were there who probably thought, "Look, they're releasing them. They're about to release them." That sort of thing. So I asked him not to do that sort of thing, but rather we should focus on our principal assignment to organise the groups within the barracks, form a convoy, set up a security system, and take these people to Sremska Mitrovica where they were supposed to be taken. There would be further screening there, further processing, interrogations, and it would be easy enough once there to ascertain who was a war criminal and who was blameless. That's what I asked him at the time, that we should get those people out of there, in order to avoid causing any further irritation to the TO men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him what exactly had gone on to the barracks previous to your departure? Did you tell him about that? Who was there, what happened, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Needless to say, it was for that reason that I asked him the things that I asked him. I told him I had been encountering some difficulty with those people, that they had followed me all the way, that they had got as far as the barracks to make clear their displeasure and virtually physical attack those people. He seemed surprised. "What on earth were they doing there," he said. I said, "Well, there you are. They were there. We had some problems back at the barracks, and this is the very reason." And that's why I asked him to not do that sort of thing again. He was somewhat surprised that they had been behaving in that way. And I had told them [as interpreted] that there was a security system in place at the barracks. I said everything was perfectly all right in terms of that security system, that there were some tiny problems. Still, I was adamant that we shouldn't do that kind of thing again. I told him security was all right, but I also warned them that actions such as these might be a bit difficult under the circumstances that prevailed at the time in this wartime situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You described the situation you found at the hospital when you arrived there that morning. What about now? Did you notice anything different? Did you notice any changes in relation to your earlier impressions when you were standing outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The situation was that group was moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and it's not his fault. I don't know whether it's an error in the translation or not. If one looks at 40 and then 3, "I told him security was all right, but I also warned them that actions such as these might be a bit difficult." Is it a case of a warning to the TO, or is it a case that he is warning Mr. Sljivancanin? Because it's, in structure, it's illogical.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: I said "him," not them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've heard this, Mr. Vukasinovic. Please just explain who it was that you warned at the time about what you had experienced at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed Major Sljivancanin about the fact that they were there and about the sort of behaviour displayed by the TO men. I informed him and, again, I let him know that everything was fine there in terms of security, but that he shouldn't give me this sort of assignment again, in terms of sending me back there and expecting me to evacuate a group like that. I asked to stop this sort of individual intervention, but rather stick to our original tasks to take them to the barracks and from the barracks. It was in this sense that I informed Major Sljivancanin of the sort of actions taken by the TO men back at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's much clearer now. Thank you. What about my previous question: What exactly constituted the difference between this arrival and the first time you arrived outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is more displeasure being voiced now. They were using slogans, saying: "They'll be releasing the whole lot. They're protecting them, these people who had killed so many of our relatives." All sorts of things being said in a general sense of discontent or protest about this particular belief that they held at the time; namely, that we were about to release those people. So they were just voicing in the strongest terms their disagreement with the fact that Sljivancanin had released about 15 individuals. When I say "they," I mean the remaining TO men, and there were a little more of them there now in relation to their number, that same morning. They probably moved at some point from the barracks and went to the hospital. In one word, there were more of them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about inside the hospital perimeter in the courtyard, did you notice anything different happening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I watched from a distance and noticed that a number of journalists had arrived. There were quite a number of them near the hospital entrance. They were talking, which suggested to me that these press teams had arrived sometime before my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point, during that day, go to Velepromet, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally attend the SAO Baranja Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem government meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happens now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We released the persons that we released. There was that bus with three or four persons and the other two buses that were full, so three buses, a total of three buses and in other group. I took them all to the barracks. When I got there, I noticed there were no buses there. I didn't actually enter the compound. Captain Predojevic met me at the gate and said, "Major comrade." And I said, "Where are the buses?" And he said, "Major comrade, the buses have left for Ovcara." And I said, "Who gave that order?" And he said, "The commander did." And he said, "You should turn this other group around as well and head in the same direction." I was somewhat taken aback by this. But given the sort of answer that I received, I had no reason not to believe that this was now the case. So I had my buses turn around, and I drove in the direction of Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at that moment when we dealt with those 20 persons that he had released. That was the conversation we had last, and I didn't see him until that evening later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your last meeting at the hospital, did he at any point in time mention the word "Ovcara"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he mention at any point in time that there would be some changes to the plan that you had discussed the previous day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No changes whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived to the Ovcara sector with my group of buses, I saw that the first three buses, which had arrived with the first group, were empty. When I got off my vehicle -- got out of my vehicle, I saw that there were many members of the TO, also some 40 to 50 of them in front of the hangar. And I saw this larger group of people milling about the hangar, around the hangar. The hangar door was open; and as I was moving about, I saw Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, who was Chief of Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we proceed, you said that these buses were empty. Where did you park your buses, in relation to these other three buses that you've just mentioned, that had been taken there before you came, obviously?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I parked behind them in a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that I had noticed that this was outside of the regular procedure, I was surprised and I saw that there was a lot of commotion there. I was angry once again, and I turned to Lieutenant-Colonel Panic and I told him, "What is this? Who ordered this?" He looked at me in a surprised way, but he said that those were the orders. I turned around and I went straight to the hangar to see what was going on there. However, there, I saw that a group of TO members was actually inside, that the people who had been taken off the buses were in a state of fear, and that these other men were slapping them, hitting them. And I could see that those people were scared; I could see that. I concluded that that all of them were intermingled, that they had gone in, and that they started looking for the people that they wanted to find, people that they had threatened earlier. Once again, I saw the commander, the TO commander, Vujovic. And I decided to kick them all outside to establish peace and order; however, in order to do that, I decided to approach him to ask him to help me do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you see Vujovic, inside the hang or in front of it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vujovic was in front of it, outside the hangar. There, in front of the hangar, I addressed him, and I said to him, "You are their commander. Let's deal with this. Let's kick these people out. Tell your men that they are not allowed to go in and beat these people and do anything physical to these people who are under our jurisdiction."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what happened next? How did he react? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meantime, there was several policemen there from the 80th Brigade who were also scared. There were maybe five or six of them. I think that there was an officer among them, but I'm not sure. They were also fearful. I called them, and I called my policemen. I said we should go inside; and with the support of Commander Vujovic, we should deal with this, kick these people out, and make sure that the other men were left there inside alone. In my conversation with Vujovic, he had this nonchalant appearance, as though he was hesitating whether to help me or not to help me. And I went up and down and he kept saying things, "Oh, this is really nothing. I can't deal with this." But when I realised what the situation was like, I approached him and said, "Vujovic, the situation is quite serious. I ask that you help me to kick these people out.
