We didn't bring these men here so that you could beat them and judge them yourselves." He said to me, "Very well. Which people are yours and which people are ours?" That was the drift of what he was saying, and then he started helping me. And he started exerting influence over his people, and we started pushing them out until we pushed the last man out. Once I was sure that not a single one of them remained in the hangar, I brought the buses closer, the other three buses closer, because the other three I had turned in the opposite direction; and then with the assistance of the soldiers, I put on the buses the people that I had brought to the hangar. As we were boarding them on the buses, as far as I could observe, there was no beating going on. They stood there yelling, but there was no significant beating, as was the case in the first instance. Because I could see on the people -- on the -- the people who were in the hangar that some of them were bloody, confused, afraid, and that they had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. We have an intervention to the transcript, page 45, line 11. Your dialogue with Vujovic, you said something that was not a formal expression. Would you please -- and that may have caused confusion in the transcript. Can you please tell us, again, what did Vujovic say to you when you asked him for assistance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to remember his words verbatim. We argued and when I said that those were ours, he said, "No, those were their soldiers." That's what he said. And I said, "No. No, those were ours. And as long as they are under our control, you have nothing to do with them." That was the gist of our conversation. I kept insisting and telling him that they are not allowed to do that, and he should use his men to help me get these people out where they did not belong. As far as I can remember, that was the conversation that we had. I needed his support and his assistance in dealing with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as you could remember, how many TO members were there in the hangar when you entered?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were about 15 -- ten to 15 in front and then -- well, about 15. 15 to 20, thereabouts. It's difficult for me to pinpoint the exact number, but I think that that's the approximate figure. Because when we pushed them outside, I could see better how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you entered for the first time -- or rather, let me ask you this: Did you enter the hangar more than once?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the hangar until we kicked them all out. When we pushed them all out, I was in front of the hangar. And I stood there until we made sure that the doors were closed and that we put security detail in front, and then I stood in front of the hangar talking to Vujovic about the need for him to remove his people from the area because their presence irritated the other people and put people at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Lieutenant-Colonel Panic later on as well? Was he there throughout your contacts with Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After that initial contact I had with Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, he left. He didn't stay there longer. I don't know where he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during that period of time while you were in the hangar, while you were in front of the hangar, did you happen to see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may have seen that person sometimes in passing. I barely knew what he looked like. I knew that he was brigade commander; however, that was a new unit that came to our area of responsibility. I had very little -- very few dealings with that unit. I had heard of them. I knew some of them, but I had very little contact with them, didn't really know faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that any JNA officer addressed you there in that area, or did you address any of the JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is completely untrue. Nobody addressed me; and, likewise, I did not address anyone, except for Mr. Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when these TO members were kicked out, were thrown out of the hangar, what measures were taken then? What happened then in relation to the hangar and the security of persons there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, as I was talking to Vujovic, I saw that a large number of TO members withdrew. So that when I was done with that, perhaps there was a group of ten of them in the broader area around hangar; that is to say, many of them had left. Mr. Vujovic left after that, too. And I called the soldiers, who were there, telling them that they should proceed, take their positions, and ensure security. And I asked them, "How come you were doing nothing?" They were taken aback. However, when they realised that the situation calmed down, they resumed their positions and started guarding. The hangar door was closed. I told them to ensure that nobody should be allowed in without their superior officer's approval. Given the situation and what it was at that point in time, I decided to leave the Ovcara sector. I decided to get into my car, take me buses and my soldiers to Negoslavci, and I went to my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let us deal with some specific questions. My first question: Mr. Vukasinovic, can you specify how long you stayed at Ovcara on that occasion from the moment you arrived until the moment you left? How much time elapsed, and can you give us some idea about the time of the day, if you're not sure about the exact time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some of my statements, I gave some indication of time; however, once again, Your Honours, I must tell you that those indications are quite different. I can be more specific if I take into account the activities or the time of the, day but it's very difficult to say that it was at 10.00 or some other time. But I can tell you that I was there from about 1.30 to 2.00, and that I stayed there for about an hour and a half, that's my assessment. And I can't give you the exact idea. I'm just presenting you my perceptions, but I think that I left the Ovcara sector sometime at around 3.30, as far as I can remember and taking into account the activities that I had carried out. And if you also take into account what other witnesses said, then you will probably have a pretty good idea of the time that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're interested in how long you stayed. As for the exact time, we will adduce additional evidence concerning that. Let me put several brief questions to you. While you were at Ovcara, did you see any colonels there, any JNA colonels in uniform standing in front of the hangar or perhaps inside of it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wish they were there. They would have been of use to me, but there was nobody there because I would have used their presence to help me with my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, while you stood there in front of the hangar, did you see a group of civilians standing there, people who had been separated off and who had somebody guarding there, securing them there? Do you remember seeing anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there in that area, did you see a bulldozer, a digger, or a tractor or anything of that sort standing in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in the hangar, did you see that there was a rope stretched out in the hangar itself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It wasn't a bulldozer, digger, it was an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in the hangar, did you see anybody making a list of the people inside?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were there in the hangar, did you see anyone beating those people? Did you see any beating going on, kicking during your presence there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We started immediately to carry out my idea to kick them out of the hangar, and we succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in front of the hangar and inside the hangar, did you hear a whistle and some moaning after you would hear a whistle blown? Anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Kemal Ajiti [phoen] or Kemal mean anything to you? Kemal Sajiti or Kemal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that I saw one Albanian in the hangar who was apparently beaten harder than others; and since I spoke Albanian, I talked with him. I saw that he was from the same -- hails from the same region that I do. I spoke to him. He was relatively okay, although he'd been beaten. I didn't know his name, but I could see he was an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any women within the hangar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was one woman, blonde. I don't know -- I couldn't place her age, between 25, 30. I'm not sure whether she was any older than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in that area, within and in front of the hangar, were you approached by anybody asking to be allowed to take some persons out of the hangar? Were you approached personally?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how Vezmarevic Dragan looks like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From conversations I heard that that gentleman was a company commander, but I never set my eyes on him. Maybe I did see him. But I was never introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the period while you were at Ovcara, and you stated how long you stayed there, did you at any point see Veselin Sljivancanin in the area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So after the situation calmed down, I arrived at Negoslavci, went to my command post. There, I briefed my deputy; he briefed me about some current affairs. I rested a bit; and before the evening briefing, I went to see the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go to see your commander, which commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the command post, to see commander, Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For what reason?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the marching route had been changed, that there'd been problems at Ovcara, it was my duty to brief the commander of the changes that had not been known to me. I entered the hall, addressed my commander, and literally, I said, "Colonel comrade, I was at Ovcara. People are lodged there. I had some problems with the Territorial Defence members. I calmed down the situation. They departed somewhere. I proposed that we strengthen security detail there, because I have a feeling that there might be some problems in the future." As I said just now, the commander listened me out and said, "Vukasin," this is how they called me, "you may go." And then upon that, I left the command post and went to my command post. This is what I felt I had to tell the commander about the situation that I had described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, on that evening, did you, and when did you see Mr. Sljivancanin? And if so, what is your recollection of that meeting with him or conversation you had with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, he was late in the briefing that evening. He passed by my command post. We saw each other for a couple of seconds. I told him that I'd been to Ovcara, and he was in passing, he said, "I'm late going to the briefing." After the briefing, he summoned me, I think. I briefed him on developments; and at the time when I was telling him that there had been people at Ovcara, he was surprised at the location they were taken to. Then I referred to him the problems that I'd encountered, and I told him that the situation had been sorted out. He answered, "Yes, okay. I knew that you would carry out your task, that you would protect the people. Well done." And that was it. And he said that he would probably look into it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, and when did you hear that there was a government session at Vukovar that day, and do you have any information about that government session?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that government session only after I had returned to my command post. Because en route, and while dealing with these problems, I was cut-off from any information. I didn't know anything. But when I arrived to my command post, my deputy told me, "Boss, there was going to be a government session," as he'd heard, "and that some very important decisions for us are going to be taken at that government meeting." I asked him, "What kind of decisions?" And he said that he'd heard about the government session, that we now had our army, and that all the prisoners would be in their care. I asked him, "Where did you get this information from?" And he answered that there'd been a press release on the radio, and that he'd heard people talk about that in the command post area. And this is all I learned about that government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you refresh our memory as to the -- your deputy's name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Bozic Mile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This all takes place on your command post -- the command post of the Negoslavci village?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After returning from Ovcara, did you ever go back to Ovcara before you left Vukovar altogether?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, in the following days, did any representatives of the International Red Cross arrive to Negoslavci? Do you know of any of them possible meetings with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st, it seems to me, they arrived, I mean the International Red Cross representatives, and they had a meeting. I believe that Major Sljivancanin was with them at the time. Probably he was, I'm not sure, but I think it was him who was accompanying them. But I know that they were there because my gate service registered their arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were your activities in the following days, and when did you leave Vukovar altogether, generally speaking, roughly, if you may recall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My activities were focused mainly on preparations for a return to Belgrade, which means the command post of the OG South had to be evacuated, which means preparations had to be made to move the command post. I was supposed to provide security and hand it over to the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, which means that we had to prepare everything for secure dislocation and withdrawal of command and all units from the area of Negoslavci towards Belgrade, and handing over the areas of responsibility to others, and introducing and inducing the new officer, showing him the ropes, main communications, brief him on the problems that we'd encountered, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that the brigade left the Negoslavci-Vukovar area on the 24th of November. During your stay there, could you tell us whether you heard any stories about the people at the hangar. If so, what were the stories?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, on the 21st, I was flooded with many tasks. I was back at my command post. Many decisions passed through me. I had to be involved. My deputy was there to tour the control points. He commanded his own units. And on one occasion, he returned from an inspection tour; and, in passing, he told me, well, since I was not his permanent but temporary commander, he just nonchalantly said that, "Boss, we heard that the people from Ovcara disappeared overnight. They were taken away or liquidated." I heard this from him, but I couldn't believe that something of the sort might be possible. At that time, while combat operations were underway, there were many rumours flying around. It was a war of misinformation. I believed this to be a rumour implanted among many others that were sent. I heard some children had been roasted at Borovo Naselje, that some babies were slaughtered. Many people had been found killed in the landfill at Vukovar, and I thought that this was just another rumour of the same sort and I simply disbelieved it. I kept this information in my head, but nobody subsequently had confirmed that this had happened; and a couple of days later, I simply stopped thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I do not have any more questions. But if we were to take a break now, I would go through my notes; and then if we were to come back from the break five minutes earlier, I may have some other questions for him because this is a very important witness. So can we move the break a bit forward before I hand this witness to my learned colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Lukic. We will adjourn now for lunch and resume at five minutes before 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a clarification on two issues and two questions, and I'm going to be over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Vukasinovic, we were dealing with the rumours that you heard. You said that you heard from your deputy, from whom and when did you hear those rumours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard those rumours on my command post from my deputy Captain Bozic, from Captain Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you relate this to Mr. Sljivancanin, those rumours that you heard?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I thought that this was impossible. I really took those to be rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And just one more question. On that day, when you were at Ovcara, and later on when you returned to the command post at Commander Mrksic's, did you at any point see Captain Karanfilov?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no contacts with him, no need to contact, and I state here that I was not in contact with that captain, neither at Ovcara nor at the hospital. I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hereby confirm that I've finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Vukasinovic. I'm going to examine you on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Mrksic, and the same instruction still holds that you make a pause between question and answer so that everything can be stated for the record. Thank you. Answering to my colleague Lukic's question, you said that on the 19th in the evening, Mr. Sljivancanin, at the meeting of security organs, told you about the evacuation of the hospital and told you about the tasks that you were about to carry out on the 20th, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did he tell you also that the task concerning the evacuation of the hospital was determined at the regular briefing at the brigade commander's office, and that it elaborates further at the security organs meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in that sense; to wit, he did not explain who is about to do what, meaning the task from that meeting. He simply stated that my task was this and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that evening, did Mr. Sljivancanin tell you that persons that may be separated as participants in an armed insurrection or perpetrators of a crime were supposed to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica, and that that was an order of the OG South, the OG South command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that my task was with regard to those separated people who may be located at the hospital to be transported to the barracks, the barracks of Vukovar, from where they would be sent by convoy to Sremska Mitrovica. Where did he receive that information? That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to my colleague Lukic's question, you stated that you provided a statement to the OTP on the 16th of November, 2002; it was signed on the 26th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether you stated to the OTP investigators -- and that would be page 0115264. I would like to ask the usher to provide the witness with a set of these statements, and I would also like to bring on to the screen the English version, page 5 of 10 of this, and the number is 01152269.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just interrupt for a moment. My learned friend, Mr. Vasic, asked whether he could use the statements that we had prepared before lunch, inquired before lunch about that. We didn't have them. I have a set prepared with indexes; and if my learned friend wants to use them, rather than me produce them now, I'm quite happy for them to be given to the Defence and the Bench so that there is an element of continuity. I'm sorry for changing this. I just now have access to them. Would that help?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thanks to my learned colleague from the OTP. Maybe this would be a useful for continuity purposes and for the transcript, because my learned colleague is going to cross-examine on the basis of the same documents. Thank you for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just assist my learned friend and the Court and indicate just exactly the way they are structured? It's not terribly difficult but it will help my friend, Mr. Vasic, who's not seen it before. Might I be permitted to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be helpful, Mr. Moore, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one just goes to the very front, one can see the index. There are 12 tabs; it's the customary route that we take. The B/C/S version, the date of the document is clearly particularised. I'm sorry it's in English, not B/C/S. Number 2 is the original B/C/S for the 16th of November, 1998. Number 4 is the 21st of December; that's B/C/S. Again, if we move down, number 6, 16th and 26th of November, 2002. Then we have got number 8, 28th of November, 2003. And number 10, 16th of December, 2004. And then we have the final statement at the Belgrade district court, 11th of November, number 12. They all, and I hope they are, in chronological order, and the English are the other tabs. I hope that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was very useful, of course. And given that we all have these documents before us, I would like to ask the usher when I invoke a document, to have it brought in the B/C/S version to e-court for the benefit of the witness, and the rest of us are going to use the English version. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the document that I referred to previously, and that would be tab 6, Mr. Vukasinovic. That would be page -- or rather, paragraph 16. For the benefit of the Bench and my learned colleague, so tab 5, paragraph 16, on page 4 of 10 in the English version. Mr. Vukasinovic, does this paragraph state that security organs in the Guards Brigade had regular tasking throughout the combat activities and, "among other things, our tasks included the evacuation of prisoners of war from Vukovar." Is it what you stated to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you mention the telegram from Aleksandar Vasiljevic and the election of prisoners for an exchange; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On that evening, did Mr. Sljivancanin say to you what the transport route should be? You stated today it should take you first to the barracks, and then could you explain the route from the barracks onwards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, I stated that my area of responsibility was -- rather, my task, when I became commander of the command post of Negoslavci, was to secure convoys. Now I'm -- what I'm referring to is that my involvement was well justified in this matter, because I had the forces that dealt with such tasks and that my involvement was fully justified. The basic goal, as I stated already, was to separate suspects who had no place in the hospital, in terms of security so that we could perform the basic task and that would be the evacuation of the infirm and injured from the hospital. And that was the task of the command as a whole, and the command that was tasked with that will give out tasks to its component elements. And our basic duty within that structure was to take security measures to carry out the basic task. Why? Because in the hospital, there were indications and intelligence that a large number of HDZ members, who did not want to surrender, disguised themselves as patients and purported to be infirm or that they were hospital staff. And given that the in the meantime, we had received information that there was continued need to take measures against the groups that threatened action against command posts in the rear, or some dislocated units of ours; therefore, we had the task for those who did not belong to the hospital as a neutral facility, to separate those so that this may not ingender further problems, so that these members would not perform attacks against our units or people from other units. And this was the task of the security organ to perform a triage to separate these from the rest of the population, to separate and transport these from the hospital toward the barracks. And the 1st armoured company was in charge of that, to organise a convoy at the barracks, secure the column, and dispatch it towards Sremska Mitrovica. That was the gist of the task that was handed to me by him and as I understood it and as I was about to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you were given this task that evening, did you plan the number of vehicles that you needed to secure the convoy? How many patrols you needed for that purpose, and why did those vehicles and patrols -- why did they not form a convoy directly from the hospital towards Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an elaborate tactics for that. It was prearranged. I did that at my command post in terms of securing any sort of convoy. We had two combat vehicles; one at the point, one at the rear. These were the measures that we had prepared at all times. Why didn't we go from hospital straight to Sremska Mitrovica? Well, the hospital is a neutral facility where we had a very complex situation with different categories of persons still not defined. It was impossible to secure that place. And practice has borne us out that the barracks should be the place where we should do that, because it was under our control that, in security terms, it was -- provided the greatest level of safety, that we had enough manpower at the barracks, and that we could prepare everything necessary at the barracks and task somebody to organise a convoy to take it to Sremska Mitrovica. And that was our basic intention; to use the barracks as a place which provided us with the greatest level of security at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether you think that that security estimate, with regard to the barracks, was appropriate in terms of safety of the personnel, the way that you just described?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I agree with this statement. There was no better facility that could be found in the area at that moment for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: May I remind you - and I believe that you answered to my friend Lukic's question - that two days before that, there was a number of convoys departing from Vukovar; one on the 18th from the Mitnica prisoners, then a convoy of civilians that was returned from Lipovac on the motor way, which passed through the Ovcara hangar. Did you think that the Ovcara hangar was a more secure place than the barracks at that moment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in my opinion. In the first case, it is only logical that Ovcara was used because activities were taking place in that axis, and the hangar was the most appropriate place. But on this axis, this would not be an appropriate facility because here, along this axis, we have an advance command post. You know what that is? Most of the command is put in a forward position. We have a unit which has the manpower and the conditions to secure any activity at the barracks, and the barracks is located adjacent to the route of withdrawal and it's closest to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When my learned colleague Lukic asked you this question, you explained what you did on the 18th of November. What I want to know is whether, on the 18th of November, you actually saw Mr. Mrksic at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw each other every day because I was there, and this is a very difficult question. Of course I saw had him, but I don't know at what time. I don't know what you're aiming at, but I'm sure we did see each other on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because as far as I understand it, you did not attend the regular briefings. Because Mr. Sljivancanin, who was the chief of the security organ, he attended them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not attend those briefings, but I could have gone to the command post. And I could have come and seen my commander and to have a chat with him or perhaps to carry out a task that he would give me, so I was not prohibited from going to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 20th, you actually went to the command post, and you explained to us what you spoke about with Mr. Mrksic, that was in the afternoon of the 20th. Did you see him later on during that day or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw my commander on that occasion; and later on, I did not see him again. I don't know at what time my commander actually left; but after this briefing, I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, you are given this task. You come with six buses in front of the hospital, and you told us who you found there in front of the hospital. Did you encounter Captain Karanfilov in front of the hospital? You told us that you did not see him at the barracks and at Ovcara, but did you see him there at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a statement, I stated that I did see him. But I have to say now from this vantage point that I may have seen him, but I'm not sure anymore. I stated at one point that I had seen him, but now I can no longer be sure. I'm sort of undecided. I don't know whether I had seen him or not. I have this feeling that I did see him, but I cannot be sure. So I cannot really give you a decisive answer. As far as I can recall at this point, I may have seen him but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you may have seen him, but you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You assigned the soldiers from the 2nd Battalion of the military police who would escort the convoy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not assign them; I was given those soldiers. So they were actually assigned to me, and they came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you put these soldiers on to the buses, and did you tell them how many soldiers per each bus, and did you instruct them what they were to do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I put the soldiers on to the buses, and I gave them their task. I told them that they were supposed to secure the people who were loaded on to the bus, to assign places to them on the bus, and we basically decided who would do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And while you were there in front of the hospital, did those soldiers, were they on the buses all the time, or were they also in the hospital compound? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were on the buses at all times, and they could get off only when I told them to. They sat in the front seats on all the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that you had first filled three buses and that then you had taken those three buses to the barracks. Did you get the task from Mr. Sljivancanin to head towards the barracks with those three buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I stated in my statement, I decided to take the buses there because in the meantime, there was no need for them to just stand there. This whole area was rather narrow, and I decided to move the first group towards their destination, which was the barracks, in order to have more manoeuvreing space and space for the activities that were to follow, the evacuation of the sick and wounded. So I decided to move them from there. That was my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at the statement that you had given to the military court, that would be at tab 4, or 3 for my learned colleagues and Your Honours. I'm interested in page 3 in B/C/S and the English that would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist my learned friend, to assist my learned friend, what I have done with the English is -- and I think the Court should have it. You should have the B/C/S page number on the English. Therefore, if my learned friend calls out the B/C/S number, we will be able to see which English page it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that would be page 3 in English, too. This is the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's at tab 4. The B/C/S version is at tab 4 and the page is page 3, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It says here -- I mean you say, "First, I transported one group of 150 people from the hospital in Vukovar to the Vukovar barracks around 1000 hours, pursuant to the order issued by Major Sljivancanin." Do you remember stating that to the investigating judge of the military court?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this group, was it transported there on the orders of Mr. Sljivancanin in accordance with what -- the conversation that you had had in the evening of the 19th regarding the evacuation of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a task that was given in the evening of the 19th, so this sentence probably relates to this. This, of course, would also depend on the actual question that the investigating judge asked me; but if you insist, this is generally true. But in terms of who actually took this decision, in that specific instance, I made this decision to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me how long were you in the hospital? So from the moment when you arrived there with six buses until the moment where the three buses were full of people and you headed out towards the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess that it took until 3.00 at the barracks. So we spent there about three hours and then the first group headed out. That's my guess, three hours, three and a half hours, thereabouts. And from my command post, I headed out at around 6.00. So that all told, I think I can see -- I think that it may have been around 10.00 that we actually arrived at the barracks, as I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you did in those four hours? So actually, if you headed out at 6.00 from Negoslavci, it would take you about 45 minutes to get there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So what did you actually do, you and your soldiers you, who there on and around the buses, in the three hours and 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were waiting for all the activities to be completed; the triage, the searches. It takes a long time for all of that to be done. A certain time is needed to do that, to separate those people. And we simply stood there and waited for those people to be ready. It's a very serious situation to carry out a search of such a person. There is a special methodology. And when you're dealing with a hospital, when you have people that are sick, who are wounded, I guess that this time was taken to actually carry out all those activities. And I was simply waiting for them to be ready for me to take them on, for all those activities to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you took on those persons, when they were ready to be handed over to you, did this mean that triage was over, or did the triage continue while you were travelling on the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The triage was over in terms of the separation of people within the hospital. But in terms of the identification of those people and any further analysis, this was to be done in Sremska Mitrovica. But as far as our part of the task was concerned, that was over and done with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now let me make this clear: Does this relate to all the people that were supposed to be triaged at the hospital or just the group that you had taken away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerned also the other group. So the triage was to be over for me to be able to take them all to the barracks, and then their identification and interviews would be carried out at Sremska Mitrovica. Our service had intelligence on those groups and individuals, and probably their status would be decided there; who would be held there and who would be released. This was not something that we had the power to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So if the whole group was triaged, why did you then not take all the five or six buses on, if the whole group had already been dealt with? Is there any particular reason for that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason. There simply were no conditions to do that. The first group was over, and the second group was in the process of being processed. And I didn't want to wait for the second group to be over, so that was simply the only reason. I just wanted to move these people out so that they don't cause any irritation. Because as the day progressed, there would probably be even worse problems if you had all the six buses full of people just standing there. I think it would have interfered with the evacuation of the sick and wounded, because it was a very narrow area. For this reason, I simply told myself, "Well, this a part it over now. Let's take these people now to the barracks," and I assumed that the second group would be smaller. And it turned out to have been the case, and I think it was not a mistake to do that. One could do either this or that, and I decided to do what I actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After you went to the barracks - and this is what you said to Captain Predojevic who was surprised at first, but then you explained to him what he would do and how he should go about securing the buses - do you know whether Captain Predojevic had informed Mr. Lukic, the barracks commander, about that? I think his rank was major.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't know if that was the case, but Captain Predojevic was duty-bound to secure the people who had come to his barracks. That was -- the barracks was his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While you were in the barracks with the three buses, who actually secured the people who were on the process of triage and who were being put on the remaining buses at the hospital? So who was securing these people at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two police officers per bus. We had the unit that was securing the hospital. So there were no problems, in fact, that would have affected the security of the these people. And after all, this was a very short time, because I came back within an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you know who authorised this group - you said that there were TO members - to actually get into the barracks compound? Did the barracks not have its own secured, the guards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the question that should be answered by the barracks commander. I could not give you an answer to that, because it is the responsibility of the barracks commander; the functioning of all the relevant organs within his barracks. The barracks had its organs, and that is a fact; and of course it -- its fence, it has to have a fence. But the fence was quite badly damaged, and the soldiers were assigned according to the assessment of the commander. You didn't have enough soldiers to actually close off all the entry points. And the organs that were assigned to those tasks probably did not do their job properly, and they could not prevent the TO members from actually entering the barracks compound. This is something that is within the responsibility of the barracks commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You ordered Mr. Predojevic to use his forces to expel the TO members and establish order in the barracks, and you did that -- he did that; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, I ordered him to see to it that the buses couldn't be opened or anybody -- so that nobody would be able to go on the buses or for the bus doors to be opened. In principle, that was his basic task. Later, with other forces - and this is something that I didn't actually order him. It was his commander, Susic, who did that - but the second order was for them to remove these people from the barracks. My basic purpose was to protect the people, and that is what I insisted on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it was Susic that ordered Predojevic to carry out this action of removing these people? When did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that out in talking with my colleagues. Well, you know, you cannot be a witness without asking people anything or without having any documents. Actually, what jogged my memory was when I received some documents. After so many years have passed, you cannot remember all the details. So in these talks, we actually found out who did what, and I found out that this part of the task was executed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you find that out, can you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your answer has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the Belgrade Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that Mr. Susic, at that time, was not Captain Predojevic's superior, when such an assertion would actually be pointless?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question at all. What do you mean he was not his superior? Before my testifying in the Belgrade Ovcara case, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that this time, that we are talking about the 20th of November, the 2nd Company, captain of the 1st Battalion of the military police, Captain Predojevic's unit; in other words, had been attached to the 2nd Assault Detachment and was under the command of the -- its commander, Major Lukic. Of course this does refresh your memory. Actually, you will tell me that that was the way it was; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now it is quite clear now. You are asking me things that were not within my remit. Why he returned to his former -- or just happened to be there with his superior, now that is a question of their relationship. This is something I have no way of knowing, and I have no way of influencing any relation of theirs; Predojevic and Susic, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And who told you that Predojevic actually approached Susic? Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. After the first two statements that we have given; one to the security administration, the other to the military court, we saw that some things needed -- that we needed to refresh our memories about some things. And so in so doing, we actually talked about some of these activities, because one has no way of knowing or remembering everything. So we talked amongst ourselves, as interlocutors, as collaborators, as friends. And these days, not these days, but before the Belgrade Ovcara case, which was sometime in the summer of 2003, that was when we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, had ordered Captain Predojevic to secure the buses and not to let anyone near the buses? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you see the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, then, at the barracks at the time when those buses were there and when the members of the TO were around the buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that in 2005, I suppose after these consultations that you have just described, in your testimony in the case of the accused Sasa Radak on the 11th of November, 2005. This is binder 12 and the tab number in the English is 11, the page being 8/24 in the B/C/S. In English, the page is -- please bear with me, I need a little time to find the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If my learned friend tells the page number top right-hand corner of the B/C/S, we can find it on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 06042901. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you look at the last paragraph. You are referring to the barracks, and you say there the worse situation was in the barracks; probably that first meeting with the rivals, when they recognised them and that one killed my father, one killed my so and so, and so on. Is this conclusion, which you adduced at the trial in Belgrade, is this a product of the exchange of information that you referred to a while ago; this exchange with your colleagues, who had been at Vukovar in the time under review, or was this purely your own judgement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Namely, this is solely my own position; my own view of the situation that obtained. And when I said pulling out of these 20, that was even worse because they thought that I meant that we would be liberating them. And that is why they were all the more aggressive and all the more angry with me, and that is what accounted for their conduct. This is the way I saw the situation myself. This is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: According to your position, the situation in the barracks was worse than at the hospital and later at Ovcara, was that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The worst situation was at Ovcara. At the hospital, there were no problems. There were problems in the barracks; but in the barracks, no one sustained any blows, except for us who were transferring these people, but these were mere slaps, more or less. But the worst, most difficult situation was at Ovcara. There, there were problems that I couldn't take care of, because I wasn't there. But once I got there, I could see what kind of problems they had, because I could see it on the peoples' faces, from the way the people looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But why then did you say that the worst situation was in the barracks? You did not say that the worst situation was at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm stating officially, before this Court, that the worst situation was there, and perhaps that was a slip of the tongue before. I'm now answering your question in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, are you certain that you were issued a task that evening by Major Sljivancanin to first take the people to the barracks, and then to set up this convoy to transport them to Sremska Mitrovica? According to testimonies that we have heard here, this decision crystalised only the following morning; namely, that the convoy should first be dispatched to the barracks. Does this change anything in your recollection, or do you still adhere to your version of how events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not changing anything. The task which I was given was such, and I don't see any other position. Namely, that was my position, that was my task, that is what I was issued. All these assumptions and thoughts are something that is alien to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the security of this convoy to be, according to your plans, and how did you propose to make lists of these people that were going to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did not do -- let me retell you this. Some others prevented me from doing that. Now, who these others were, that is something they change the course of my action.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No. No, I asked you when? When were you supposed to make these lists?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness and counsel please not overlap because the interpreter is not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two combat vehicles; one heading the column, the other at the end of the column. There was traffic patrol to regulate, traffic on the road, according to our methods by intervening in front of the column when needed and so on. Now, when it comes to lists, I had foreseen that the lists should be prepared, drawn up in the barracks. However, that being impossible, given the technology and the regulations that we had to observe; namely, lists can be drawn up either in the barracks or on the move. But once we arrive at our destination, Sremska Mitrovica, lists had to be drawn up and persons delivered according to a list. Now, it is not written anywhere where responsible people would be drawing up those lists. They can do so whilst moving at the start of the journey; but at end, they have to deliver the persons according to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That was my question. I assumed that at a certain point, it had been envisaged that a list so being transported would have to be drawn up, because it would be quite unnatural to actually lead these people without a list; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, lists needed to be drawn up, so that we would know what was being handed over and what was being taken over. That's not where the problem lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that such lists were also drawn up when the Mitnica group was taken -- handed over, which departed on the 19th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that that was so, and I know their exact number. Namely, under conditions which are normal and securing such actions, these are things which one could not skip over. That is a normal activity in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, when you were given the task to separate off some persons in the barracks and return them to the hospital, how did you plan to secure the buses which remained in the barracks? Who did you put in charge of controlling -- of ensuring the security of those buses which would remain in the barracks until you returned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That task was Captain Predojevic's task. From the very outset until the end, that was his obligation. And when there is the military police there and it is our facility and our structures, they know what these steps and measures and activities that they need to take are. There is no need to issue any specific instructions to that effected. So in my book, that was a solved problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on arrival at the barracks -- sorry, on arrival at the hospital, were two loaded buses there waiting for you, and were they awaiting for a decision on your part to set off towards the barracks? In other words, why didn't they go to the barracks on their own before that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So persons boarded the buses; they were on the buses. They had to wait for me. I was the responsible person. No other person could have taken them to the barracks. They had to wait for me. My soldiers knew that, those who are under my command, and they waited for me to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 77, row 18. He said that my soldiers knew that temporarily, "my soldiers," and the interpretation in the transcript is something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vukasinovic, how long did you take from reaching the barracks with the first three buses until the other three buses arrived at the barracks? Can you recall how much time elapsed until the entirety of the convoy reached the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- the problem is that the whole convoy never reached the barracks. I said that I reached the barracks around 10.00, then I had to carry out the subsequently given to me task, which took me around one hour, then I went back to the hospital. I presume that I set out from the hospital around 12.30, 1.00 p.m., around that time. I'm certain it wasn't before 1.00, so around 1.00 p.m. I presume that that was the time. As I already stated, it's very difficult for me to pinpoint the exact time. But gauging by certain activities that I had to carry out, I presume I must have been there for an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If the buses that were already at the hospital site were already filled with people, what did you spend this one, one and a half hours on, while waiting for them to start, to set off?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. I'm not sure whether you listened to me. 20 people had to be released and to say to them, "You are free to go," but it wasn't down to somebody saying to them that. I was there listening to conversations conducted by Major Sljivancanin on a case-by-case basis, so at least one hour was spent that or even more. It wasn't as simple as it may look now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you reach Ovcara, approximately, please? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous statements, I put that around 1.30, 1.00, 1.30 p.m., on average that would be the time that I specified. I believe it may vary, but not much; around 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP investigators, do you recall - if not, we may consult your statement - you said that you saw Chief of Staff Miodrag Panic, and you said that you thought he left Ovcara at around 1.00, which means that you had to arrive earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are approximate time indications. I did not invent him. He had to be there when I arrived. I'm very difficult to pinpoint the exact time, but he was there when I arrived. And this is for certain, and this is true, and I believe that your [as interpreted] witness may have confirmed that or not, I cannot really say. But what I can testify to is that I encountered him there, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that maybe the witness would have confirmed, but this is not my witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel and witness not to overlap. Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To explain for the transcript, the witness said: Whether another witness confirmed that or not, he did not know. But in the transcript, page 79, line 12, it says that "your witness," whereas the witness never used the pronoun "your."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, how long did Chief of Staff Miodrag Panic stay at Ovcara while you were there? Obviously, he had arrived prior to your arrival.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he arrived. But after I approached him, to the effect that what was going on and why were you here, he answered and he immediately left after one minute's conversation with me. I approached him, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take your statement to the OTP, tab 6 of the B/C/S version and tab 5 for the English version. And if you could please find paragraph 35. Have you managed to locate it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The same page is in English. It says here: "The POWs that are brought to Ovcara were placed in the hangar in my presence; and on that occasion, no one was physically abused or harassed. I do not know whether this was the case with the previous group, because I was not present then. I think that all those placed in the hangar were supposed to stay there one day at the most, in order to do some checking and then to be transported to Sid or Sremska Mitrovica. As it had been done previously with those who were captured and detained at Ovcara." You stated that to the OTP's investigators; is that correct? Could you, for the benefit of the transcript, say something?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what, did you ascertain that they had to stay there for one day for verification or checking purposes and that they were supposed to be sent to Sremska Mitrovica, as had been done with the previous group that had been located and lodged at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the question put to me, but this is my personal thinking. When weighing everything, I presumed that the change of direction or destination had to have some reason and the same way that we kept the Mitnica group overnight, that we -- this would be the case in -- if it had started being wintertime, dusk fell very early. And this was my thinking that we had a large hangar to accommodate those people, and my thinking was that they had to spend the night there. And they would set off in the morning, presuming that the methodology of processing of these people would be the same as in the case of the previous group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the group that had already entered the hangar were guarded by the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: They were doing so in the same way that they did in the case of the previous group from Mitnica on the days 18th to the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you, what was the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't know. But roughly, judging by where they were located, maybe Ovcara and the wider area. But that was determined by the commander of the OG South through his decisions and orders, and it could be ascertained there. It is not up to me to comment on the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that you interpreted that when you were -- testified at the Belgrade district court on the 11th of November? Would you like me to confront you with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not draw up the demarcation lines between zones of responsibility. If you mean that, I did not know that. But if the command was at Ovcara, probably Ovcara was within their area of responsibility. But now the question is the scope of their area of responsibility, at what -- at any rate, where the command is located, that is probably within its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it be normal that some -- a unit would guard prisoners of war within the area of responsibility of that unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this would be one of the main tasks. They had a unit of military police that was tasked to carry out such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, given that you stated that you had not seen Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic or that you didn't know him, does that mean that -- or rather, did you see any officer around the hangar at Ovcara or within the hangar, apart from Lieutenant-Colonel Panic at the time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic. I can state that with full responsibility. I said in my statement that there was a captain there at the time of my arrival. Whether that captain was the one mentioned, Captain Vezmarevic, it doesn't mean anything to me. I saw a captain there and nobody else, in terms of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In accordance with your testimony, you, together with that captain, managed to introduce some order at the Ovcara hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I introduced order at the hangar thanks to the Commander Vujovic. He is more to be credited with that than anybody else, and of course his men and the soldiers that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When order had been established at Ovcara, was any security detail of the hangar set up, and where were the POWs at that time? Could you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had problems with POWs and people separated from the general population. I believe that the prisoners of war is too harsh a term; but if you say it so, they, and nobody else, were contained in the hangar. The hangar was closed. We had the 80th Brigade military policemen in front. There was security detailed in front of the hangar and around it, and they were tasked with securing the hangar. After all that had been put in place, I insisted that they take their posts and to secure the people inside and to prevent all other personnel from entering the hangar. This was their task throughout, and I just reminded them that they had this task which they had to carry out before the status of these people within is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they have enough manpower to do so, or did they ask for reinforcement from you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not ask any troops from me. They had enough manpower to secure that hangar. They had a company of military policemen with three platoons. A company is 100 troops strong. These were military police in national -- doing their national service, and converted into reserve. They had been mobilised. They were experienced men who could carry out this task with no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would it be the right time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We could, Mr. Vasic, if that would be convenient to you or we could go on until half past.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it would be convenient to take the break now, if possible, but I will of course be guided by your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now, Mr. Vasic, and resume at a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just indicate one small matter? I've spoken to my learned friend Mr. Borovic and his learned colleagues. There is an issue to be raised in respect of Witness 002. That might take a little bit of time and I wonder if it is possible after cross-examination today, which I believe will finish close to 5.00 or the witching hour, which is 5.00, which the matter could be raised then, at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we know anything of this, Mr. Moore or is this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I think the curtain will be raised at -- it's just to assist the Court. It's to do about the notebook, the location of the notebook, the translation of the book of 002. And I think it's a case of looking for judicial guidance in relation to what the Defence require done. And if it's going to be done, it should be started now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, we will see how the evidence progresses, and you think it will take five minutes or more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's Mr. Borovic, Your Honour. I would think at least ten or 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Five. Thank you, Mr. Moore. I think Mr. Borovic owes you one now. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps I can make things easier, because I'm nearing the end of my examination. So there will be enough time for my learned colleagues to pursue this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukasinovic, I would like to clarify one matter. In the cross-examination, I've already asked you about a portion of your statement relating to the persons that you had brought to Ovcara yourself. Did you see that these persons that you had brought in, in the three buses, as you described to us, had been abused or mistreated or beaten by anyone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not beaten because I had taken measures; in other words, I placed my soldiers in front of the hangar and they formed the gauntlet, so they could not run into the hangar and beat people. And that is how actually they went into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in the course of the Vukovar operations, that the -- whether the soldiers were warned about the rules of international law, whether in the case that they are taken captive or if they capture any enemy soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that an order to this effect was issued by the commander of the OG South. There was some guidelines and some orders from the 1st Military District; and we, as professional soldiers, had the right and the duty to train our soldiers and to teach them about combat activities and about the conduct -- the compliance with the Geneva Conventions, the laws and customs of wars so that conscripts and professional soldiers in our unit, the Guards Brigade, before they went into combat, had been fully briefed about this. And they were aware of their rights in case of capture, and also what they had to do if they captured any enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukasinovic. I have another question for you. I would now like you to take this binder and to open it at tab 10, that would be tab 9 in English. That's page 15 in the B/C/S version; and in English, that would be page 11. Were you able to find this, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, page 15. In fact, this is an answer that you provided to a question asked by the presiding judge, what you did after you left Ovcara. This is what this is all about and you say, as follows: "So order was imposed; and it was all, you know, order was instilled. They went through some phases. They even laughed at times. Sometimes, as they say, something came over them, they would become extremely aggressive and so on. But in essence, we somehow managed to calm that down." "After that, when I was done with all that, I went to my command post. Of course after the short break when I had lunch and so on, I went to the command. It was about 5.00, half past 5.00 in the afternoon, to see whether Sljivancanin was there and to simply brief him to see what the story was, why the people were there, and to tell him what the situation was. I arrived there to the operations room, the colonel, or rather, the then Major Sljivancanin was not there. The commander was there," and then you say what you told Mrksic. This is what you stated before the Belgrade court in the Ovcara case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Vukasinovic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for your answers. Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of November, 1991, when you took those people on to the buses, did Captain Miroslav Radic assist you in any way, or did he in any way participate in that activity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave a statement to the OTP stating who was present in the hospital compound on the 20th and you repeated that, and you said that you had not seen him at all there on the 20th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you brought the 20 people back to the hospital, according to this list, and you described in detail how you went from bus to bus and read out the names and counted the people, did Captain Miroslav Radic participate in those activities in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you actually never ever saw him in the barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, this completes my cross-examination -- I'm sorry, if I may just have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Captain Radic's observation post during the events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you actually don't know any of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm done now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have heard Mr. Sljivancanin being described so tall, so brave, so handsome. He had a moustache on the 20th, did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have spoken to a number of people, various institutions asking about your participation at this incident. And it would be right to say - you've now got the file in front of you - that the first time that certainly we are aware of you being spoken to was the 16th of November, 1998; is that correct? Was that the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you were summoned, the date given, is the 16th of November, 1998. Again, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You clearly must have been concerned about -- not for guilt or any reason like that, of course, but you must have been concerned about giving a statement in relation to this matter. It's not a pleasant experience, is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA VUKASINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And without putting too fine a point on it, there are many people who have expressed the view that you are a man that should have been indicted for offences here in Ovcara. You are aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to disagree with this question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
